target: General SWE / backend software engineering internships (big tech + strong startups), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
bullet_feedback.problem: 'the Claude skill' is referenced with a definite article before the reader has been told any Claude skill exists; it is only introduced in the next bullet ('splitting one large Claude skill'). 'strict access limits' is also vague: a backend interviewer cannot tell whether this means rate limits, row-level permissions, or a read quota, and that determines whether the precompute-plus-cache design was the right call.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most backend-shaped bullet at Capital One (DB constraint -> precomputed index -> cache), but a reader has to re-read it to know what is searching the tree and why, so the design reasoning is lost on the first pass.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what kind of 'access limits' (rate limit, quota, permissions) the table had
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Swap this bullet with the 65% Claude sub-skills bullet so the Claude skill is introduced first, then this bullet can say 'the skill' naturally; replace 'strict access limits' with the specific constraint type.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt the legacy tool developers use to create test-data workflows as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation, and 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it
bullet_feedback.problem: Five technology names ('React and TypeScript Electron app', 'React Flow', 'Jest') sit in the middle of the sentence, and they are all front-end; for a backend reader this leads the Capital One role with UI work and pushes the database/caching and latency bullets below it.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A backend screener reading top-down sees the Capital One role as a front-end/desktop-app internship before reaching the PostgreSQL/Redis and latency work.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder the Capital One bullets so the 65% latency bullet leads, the PostgreSQL/Redis bullet follows, and this one closes; trim to the technologies that explain the engineering (e.g. 'Electron app with a visual flow editor'), leaving React/Jest to Skills.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Automated retraining for a production Amazon Bedrock model that sorts research documents by importance: on an EventBridge schedule a larger LLM grades it, and it is fine-tuned only when those grades shift past a threshold
bullet_feedback.problem: 'a larger LLM grades it, and it is fine-tuned' uses 'it' twice for the Bedrock model, so it reads as if the LLM grades the model itself rather than the model's document rankings; the colon-then-clause structure also needs a second read.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is a genuinely interesting design (drift-triggered retraining instead of blind scheduled retraining), but the ambiguous pronouns hide that idea from both recruiters and engineers.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the larger LLM grades (the model's importance rankings on new documents)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the object of grading explicitly and put the decision first, e.g. 'retrains ... only when a larger LLM's scheduled grades of its rankings drift past a threshold'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Deployed a space-topic research tool for Amazon Leo's public-policy team and set it up for handoff with AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions CI/CD, so Leo engineers new to the project now maintain it on AWS Fargate
bullet_feedback.problem: 'space-topic research tool' does not say what the tool does (search? summarize? collect documents?), so the outcome (handoff) is clear but the system being handed off is not.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The two following bullets describe a document pipeline and a ranking model; without a one-phrase description here the reader cannot tell they are parts of the same system.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the tool does for the policy team in a few words
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'space-topic research tool' with a short functional description of the tool that ties it to the document pipeline in the next bullet.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
bullet_feedback.problem: '6,000+ scraped research documents' has no time unit, so it is unclear whether this is total corpus size or a throughput rate; 'end-to-end latency' also has no unit (per document? per batch?).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A backend interviewer will immediately ask about scale and what latency was measured; the bullet is strong but the numbers are less defensible without scope.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether 6,000+ is total or per day/week, and what unit the 34% latency refers to
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add the time scope to the document count and name what latency was measured (e.g. per-document scrape-to-inference), without adding new metrics.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Building a RAG meal-suggestion feature for the official UMD app (GPT-4o mini, ChromaDB + SentenceBERT search); 93% of generated meals rated satisfactory by internal testers
bullet_feedback.problem: The parenthetical '(GPT-4o mini, ChromaDB + SentenceBERT search)' and the semicolon splice read as a stitched tech dump rather than a sentence; the technologies are listed, not tied to what they do.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the only bullet on the page in this telegraphic form, which lowers the human-voice quality the rest of the page achieves and gives an interviewer nothing to ask about beyond the stack.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Rewrite as one sentence that says what the retrieval does (e.g. 'retrieves ... with SentenceBERT embeddings in ChromaDB so GPT-4o mini suggests ...'), and drop the parenthetical.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-founded a 110+ member student product studio that has shipped 5 live products, and personally built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for one, Tortuga, a class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
bullet_feedback.problem: Two separate stories (founding/leading a 110+ member studio and building a cache for one product) are joined by 'and', and the Redis caching has no stated reason or effect; the 20,000+ visits describes the product, not the cache.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A backend interviewer will ask why the cache was needed and what it changed; the bullet currently implies the caching drove the 20,000 visits, which an interviewer may probe.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: why Redis caching was added in front of the Prisma queries (load, latency, DB limits)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the studio framing short and make the caching clause say what problem it solved, e.g. 'built Redis caching ... so Tortuga's [reason] held up under 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days', using only the real reason.

bullet_feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project targeting ICLR, built a Python pipeline that draws AnyGrasp candidates from multi-camera images as Open3D overlays and tuned prompts so a vision-language model picks the right grasp more often
bullet_feedback.problem: 'draws AnyGrasp candidates ... as Open3D overlays' is jargon a non-robotics reader cannot restate, and 'more often' is an unanchored result.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: For a backend panel this is the least relevant bullet and also the hardest to parse; it costs reading time without adding backend signal.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether any measured improvement exists for 'more often'
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the plain purpose (helping a vision-language model choose robot grasps from camera images) and keep AnyGrasp/Open3D as secondary nouns; if no measured improvement exists, describe the outcome concretely rather than 'more often'.

page_feedback.problem: The strongest backend and cloud evidence is not what the eye hits first. The top role (AWS) has a single in-progress bullet with no result, and the most interviewable backend work (Kinesis replacing S3 staging for a 34% latency cut, CDK/CI handoff, the C++ matching engine at 1.26M events/sec) sits in the middle and bottom of the page. The AWS brand does its job in the skim, but the Capital One section then opens with a front-end Electron bullet.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A backend screener spending ~7 seconds takes away 'AWS + Capital One intern, React/Electron' before reaching the systems work that actually differentiates this candidate.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep chronological role order, but reorder bullets within Capital One so the latency and PostgreSQL/Redis bullets lead; consider whether the AWS bullet's first words can lead with the system ('Redshift capacity reservation policies for EC2') rather than 'Writing Java logic'.

page_feedback.problem: What a backend interviewer would dig into: (1) Redshift capacity bounds - how upper/lower bounds are chosen and how backtesting is set up; (2) Kinesis vs S3 - shard count, ordering, retry/poison-message handling in the Lambda consumer, and what the 34% was measured on; (3) Capital One Redis cache - invalidation when workflows change and why a precomputed category tree over a live query; (4) matching engine - the one mismatched fill out of 99,123, why std::map over an array of price levels, and how 1.26M events/sec was measured; (5) B+ tree vs LSM - write amplification and why the read-heavy result suits the workload. The page sets up all of these well, which is a strength.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: These are the follow-ups the bullets invite; the candidate should be ready, and none of the bullets claim more than they can support.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: No page change needed; keep the wording specific enough that these questions stay the natural follow-ups.

page_feedback.problem: No bullet shows designing or owning an API or service interface, even though 'REST APIs' and 'API Gateway' are listed in Skills. Most backend postings ask about API design, and the Skills line is currently the only evidence.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A backend reader looking for request/response service work sees pipelines, caches, and tools but no service boundary the candidate designed.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: If any existing project (e.g. the Amazon Leo tool on Fargate) exposes an API the candidate built, name that in its existing bullet; otherwise leave Skills as is and do not invent it.

page_feedback.problem: Skills 'Practices & Tools' line includes 'data structures and algorithms' and 'Agile', which carry no signal for a CS student and take space.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor: low-signal entries dilute the otherwise specific Skills section.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Cut 'data structures and algorithms' (and optionally 'Agile') from the Practices line.

keep: Built a C++17 order book and matching engine and replayed 50.9M real IEX exchange messages through it without ever resyncing to the exchange's book, matching 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices
Sustained 1.26M events/sec end-to-end over the full replay, with price levels in a std::map of FIFO queues and a hash map from order ID to queue position for O(1) cancels

Compared B+ tree and LSM skip-list storage for the engine's event logs on identical 2M-record workloads: the B+ tree read 12.8x faster and answered range queries 22x faster, at the cost of 27% more disk

Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting one large Claude skill into smaller sub-skills that call Python tools for search and validation, after CloudWatch and OpenSearch latency logs showed where time went

Writing Java logic that decides how much EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, setting upper and lower bounds that keep availability high without overspending, and backtesting the policies
Single-page layout, section order (Education, Experience, Projects, Technical Skills), and right-aligned dates/locations
